passage: Bhupen wanted every child in class at his party, but his parents could only host fifteen. He put his best friends and cousins at the top, counted, and cut a few names, choosing the people who mattered most. Maria came up with three ideas, a treasure hunt, a film show and pizza at home, then weighed them for price, room and enjoyment. The treasure hunt won, since it would fit in their small flat. Parveen planned five games and nothing else. She forgot food, and also how much time each game would eat up. By five o'clock the guests were hungry, and the games ran past the time when parents came to fetch them. Kiran added up the price of cake, balloons and small presents to take home and showed the list to her mother, who saw it was over what she had set aside. So Kiran gave out small pencil sets instead of gifts, and cut out paper decorations at home.

qa.q: How many guests could Bhupen's parents host?
How did Parveen's plan differ from Maria's, and what happened on the day?
qa.a: Maria compared three ideas for cost, space and fun and chose one that suited the flat. Parveen planned only games and forgot snacks and timing, so the guests got hungry and the games ran late.

qa.q: What might Parveen be feeling when parents arrive and games are still going?
qa.a: She is probably flustered and disappointed, since her guests are hungry and her party is running past the time.

qa.q: What could Parveen do the next time she plans a party?
qa.a: She could list food, timing and games together and ask an adult to look at the plan. Leaving space between games would help. 🙂

grounding: Children plan birthday parties by limiting the guest list, brainstorming and choosing, planning only games, and trimming to a budget.
